title: A 93-Year-Old Oscar Winner Sat Through 8 Hours of Indian Cinema — and Rajamouli Just Got His Name Carved Into Paris
excerpt: The Cinémathèque Française — the institution that preserved Kubrick, Hitchcock, and Kurosawa — has given India's most ambitious filmmaker a permanent seat. And it took a living legend to make it happen.
body:
Imagine this: a 93-year-old man walks into a Parisian screening room on a Saturday. He watches *RRR* — all three hours of it, the fire and water, the bridge scene, Naatu Naatu, the whole devastating thing. He tells the director he'll come back tomorrow, maybe skip *Baahubali*, just catch *Eega* instead. And then he shows up the next morning with his wife, sits down, and doesn't leave for eight hours.

That man is **Costa-Gavrás**. Oscar winner. Director of *Z* and *Missing*. One of the most important political filmmakers in cinema history. And the director who kept him rooted to his seat for an entire day? **SS Rajamouli** — from Hyderabad, India.

This past weekend, the **Cinémathèque Française** in Paris — one of the world's most revered film archives, founded in 1936 by Henri Langlois — gave Rajamouli something almost no Indian filmmaker has ever received: a permanent place in its halls. A permanent seat bearing his name. The kind of recognition that puts you in the company of the directors whose work the institution has dedicated itself to preserving since before World War II.

The honour came as part of a retrospective that screened *RRR*, *Eega*, and *Baahubali: The Beginning*, followed by a masterclass with Rajamouli himself. The event was supported by the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne and India's Ministry of External Affairs — but the moment that turned it from an industry honour into something genuinely moving was Costa-Gavrás refusing to leave.

> "The 93-year-old Academy Award winner and legendary French filmmaker Mr. Costa Gavras came to watch RRR yesterday and told SS Rajamouli that he'll come back for Eega tomorrow, skip Baahubali today. But we were surprised — he came today along with his wife and stayed 8 hours straight to watch both films and the masterclass. These are the moments that inspire us and remind why we are in cinema." — SS Karthikeya, Rajamouli's son

Eight hours. At 93. In a screening room in Paris. Watching a Telugu film about two men fighting the British Raj with their fists, and then watching a Telugu fantasy about a warrior prince lifting a golden Shiva lingam. If that's not the most extraordinary endorsement of Indian cinema's emotional power, nothing is.

Rajamouli himself was clearly overwhelmed. On X, he wrote:

> "Having me here in Paris and screening my films is itself an honour for me. But a sweet surprise I never saw coming. It is a feeling I cannot fully put into words. To have a permanent place in the halls of one of the world's most legendary film institutions, named after the great Henri Langlois himself, is something I will carry with me forever. My deepest gratitude to the legendary Mr. Costa Gavrás and the entire Cinémathèque Française family for this honour, and for embracing Indian cinema with such warmth and love."

For the Indian diaspora — the millions who have grown up watching Rajamouli's films in packed theatres from Hyderabad to Houston, from Bangalore to Birmingham — this moment carries a particular weight. Indian cinema has always been enormous at home. What Rajamouli represents is something different: the proof that Indian storytelling, at its most unapologetically epic and emotionally maximalist, can command the respect of the world's most elite film institutions. Not by making polite "festival films." Not by tailoring his voice for Western sensibilities. But by being exactly who he is — a man who makes three-hour epics about friendship, mythology, and spectacle with the absolute confidence that the emotion will translate across every border.

It helps that the emotion does translate. *RRR* didn't win the Oscar for Best Original Song by accident. The film's global run — theatrical phenomenon in Japan, viral sensation on Netflix, embraced by Letterboxd cinephiles and TikTok meme-makers alike — proved that Rajamouli's brand of cinema speaks a language that doesn't need subtitles. You feel it in your chest before you read the words.

The Cinémathèque honour arrives at a moment when Rajamouli is deep in pre-production on his most ambitious project yet: **Varanasi**, starring **Mahesh Babu** and **Priyanka Chopra Jonas**. And he used the Paris retrospective to give the European audience something no one else has seen — the very first glimpse of the film, to widespread applause from the Cinémathèque audience. Back in Hyderabad, shooting resumes July 7 for the film's centrepiece battle sequence — 50,000 CGI vanars, 3,500 physical extras, and a Paris premiere reportedly being planned for April 2027. If the Cinémathèque screening was a coronation, *Varanasi* is the promise of what comes next.

For now, though, there's a seat in Paris with his name on it. And somewhere in the 16th arrondissement, a 93-year-old man is probably still thinking about that bridge scene.
